title: NoSQL: Dynamo 2007, why people gave up relational databases, what they lost
story:
Dynamo: Amazon's highly available key-value store was presented at the ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles in October 2007. The paper describes a store used by some of Amazon's core services to provide an always-on experience, motivated by the observation that even the slightest outage has significant financial consequences and impacts customer trust.

Read that motivation carefully, because it is the whole design. The thing being optimised is not throughput or cost. It is the elimination of a particular failure — refusing a customer — and everything given up was given up for that.

The design synthesises several known techniques rather than inventing one: consistent hashing for partitioning and replication, object versioning for consistency, a quorum-like technique with decentralised replica synchronisation, and a gossip-based protocol for failure detection and membership. That is worth noting on its own. The influential paper in this lineage is an integration paper, and its contribution is the coherence of the combination and the evidence that it worked at scale.

The design space it targets is an always writeable data store, achieved by pushing conflict resolution to read time so that writes are never rejected — the motivating case being that a customer must be able to add an item to a shopping cart during partial network failures or data centre outages. A rejected write is a lost sale; a conflicting write is a problem for later. The system is built on that ordering of costs.

Now two mechanisms that are constantly conflated, and separating them is the most useful thing this lesson can do.

The first is the quorum condition. Read and write quorum sizes are configurable: R is the minimum number of nodes that must participate in a successful read and W the minimum for a successful write, out of N replicas. Setting R plus W greater than N yields a quorum-like system, because any read set and any write set must then overlap in at least one node. In practice both are often set below N for better latency.

The second is the sloppy quorum, together with hinted handoff. Rather than enforcing strict membership, a write may be accepted by healthy nodes outside the key's preference list and handed back later when the intended nodes return. This is a different mechanism from the quorum condition, and it is the one that actually keeps the store writeable during failures.

Their interaction is the part worth understanding. The overlap argument for the quorum condition assumes the write set and the read set are drawn from the same N nodes. Under a sloppy quorum they may not be — a write can be accepted by nodes that are not the key's usual replicas — so the guarantee that a read set intersects a write set does not hold in the way the arithmetic suggests. That is why this store is described as providing eventual consistency rather than strong consistency, and why the common claim that setting R plus W greater than N makes reads strongly consistent is wrong here. The quorum condition is a tunable that makes staleness less likely; it is not a guarantee, and the mechanism that makes the system available is precisely the one that breaks it.

Versions are tracked with vector clocks, each a list of node and counter pairs. When branches cannot be reconciled automatically, the store returns all of the leaves with version information in the context, and a subsequent update using that context collapses them into a single new version. For the shopping cart the reconciliation rule is the union of the conflicting versions — so a deleted item can reappear, but nothing is lost.

That detail is the honest accounting for the whole approach. Availability was purchased, and the price was paid in semantics a user can see. Nothing is lost, which was the guarantee they wanted, but nothing is lost and the cart is correct are different statements. What developers gave up is not really joins or a query language — it is having a single place where the meaning of conflicting truths is decided. That decision did not disappear; it moved into application code, where it has to be made again for every kind of object stored.

problem.name: Availability bought with merge semantics
problem.shape: A replicated store must decide what to do with a write when the intended replicas cannot be reached.
tell: the quorum condition is being cited as a consistency guarantee
conflicting versions exist and no merge rule is written down
a rejected write costs more than a stale read
availability is claimed without naming what was given up for it
problem.move: Separate the quorum condition from the sloppy quorum: the first makes staleness less likely, the second is what keeps writes accepted and is what breaks the first. Then write down the merge rule for every object type, because that rule is the consistency model your users actually experience.
problem.invariant: Never rejecting a write means accepting divergence, and divergence must be reconciled by someone. Pushing reconciliation to read time moves the decision into the application rather than removing it.
problem.breaks: Setting the read and write quorums to sum above the replica count does not make reads strongly consistent here. The overlap argument assumes both sets come from the same replicas, and the sloppy quorum that keeps the system available is precisely what allows a write to land outside them — so the mechanism providing availability is the one invalidating the guarantee.

cost.time: reads may return several versions, and the application must resolve them before it can act
cost.space: per-version metadata that grows with the number of writers, which must be truncated, at the cost of losing ordering information
cost.beats: refusing writes when replicas are unreachable, which keeps one truth and loses the customer, and a single-master design, which is simple and makes the master a point of failure and a scaling limit

worked.problem: What does setting the read and write quorums to sum above the replica count achieve, and what does it not guarantee here?
worked.reasoning:
It makes any read set and any write set overlap in at least one node, so a read is likely to see the most recent write. It does not make reads strongly consistent, and the reason is the mechanism that makes the system available in the first place.

Take the arithmetic first. R is the minimum number of nodes that must participate in a successful read, W the minimum for a successful write, out of N replicas. If R plus W exceeds N then any set of R nodes and any set of W nodes must share at least one member, so a read set contains at least one node that saw the latest write. That is the quorum-like property, and in practice both are often set below N anyway for better latency.

Now the part the arithmetic assumes: that the write set and the read set are drawn from the same N nodes. Dynamo uses what it calls a sloppy quorum together with hinted handoff — rather than enforcing strict membership, a write may be accepted by healthy nodes outside the key's preference list and handed back later when the intended nodes return.

So the write may have been accepted by nodes that are not the key's usual replicas, which means a read against those replicas can miss it entirely. The overlap guarantee does not hold in the way the arithmetic suggests. That is precisely why the store provides eventual consistency rather than strong consistency, and why the common claim that this condition delivers strongly consistent reads is wrong for this system.

The relationship is what I would emphasise, because it is the interesting bit: the mechanism that keeps the store writeable during failures is the same mechanism that invalidates the quorum guarantee. They are not two independent features with separate trade-offs — availability is bought directly out of the consistency argument. You cannot have the sloppy quorum's availability and the strict quorum's guarantee, because they are the same knob viewed from two sides.

The design context makes the choice reasonable. The paper's stated motivation is that even the slightest outage has significant financial consequences and impacts customer trust, and it targets an always writeable store by pushing conflict resolution to read time so writes are never rejected — the case being a customer adding to a cart during partial network failures or data centre outages. A rejected write is a lost sale; a conflicting write is a problem for later.

And the reconciliation is where the bill lands. Versions are tracked with vector clocks, lists of node and counter pairs, and when branches cannot be reconciled automatically the store returns all the leaves for the application to merge. For the cart the rule is union — so a deleted item can reappear, but nothing is lost.

That is the accounting for the whole approach, and it is what I would end on. What was given up is not joins or a query language. It is having one place where the meaning of conflicting truths is decided. That decision moved into application code, where it must be made again for every type of object stored — and the merge rule chosen there is the consistency model the users actually experience, whatever the quorum settings say.

problem.practice: Find a store in your stack described as eventually consistent and locate its merge rule for one object type. If nobody can tell you what happens when two writers conflict, that behaviour is still defined — by whichever write arrived last, which is a merge rule nobody chose.

beats.broke: A store that refuses writes when replicas are unreachable turns every network problem into lost customer activity, which for some workloads costs far more than serving stale data.
beats.fix: Accept the write on whatever healthy nodes can take it, track versions rather than overwriting, and push reconciliation of divergent versions to read time where the application can apply its own rule.
beats.cost: The application inherits the merge, and the merge has consequences a user can see — so correctness moves out of the store into code that must decide what conflicting truths mean, per object type.

interview.q: What does setting the read and write quorums to sum above the replica count achieve, and what does it not guarantee here?
interview.trap: Treating the condition as delivering strong consistency. The overlap argument assumes both sets are drawn from the same replicas, and the sloppy quorum that keeps the system writeable is exactly what lets a write land outside them.
interview.answer:
It makes any read set and any write set overlap in at least one node, so a read is likely to see the latest write. It does not make reads strongly consistent, and the reason is the mechanism that makes the system available.

The arithmetic: R is the minimum nodes for a successful read, W for a successful write, out of N replicas. If R plus W exceeds N, any R nodes and any W nodes share at least one member, so a read set contains a node that saw the latest write. In practice both are often set below N anyway, for latency.

What the arithmetic assumes is that both sets come from the same N nodes. Dynamo uses a sloppy quorum with hinted handoff — rather than enforcing strict membership, a write may be accepted by healthy nodes outside the key's preference list and handed back when the intended nodes return. So a write may sit on nodes that are not the key's usual replicas, and a read against those replicas can miss it entirely.

That is why the store provides eventual rather than strong consistency, and why the common claim about this condition is wrong here. The quorum condition is a tunable that makes staleness less likely, not a guarantee.

The relationship is the interesting part: the mechanism that keeps the store writeable during failures is the same one that invalidates the quorum guarantee. They are not independent features — availability is bought directly out of the consistency argument, the same knob from two sides.

The context makes the choice reasonable. The paper's motivation is that even the slightest outage has significant financial consequences and impacts customer trust, and it targets an always writeable store by pushing conflict resolution to read time so writes are never rejected. A rejected write is a lost sale; a conflicting write is a problem for later.

The bill lands at reconciliation. Vector clocks track versions, and unreconcilable branches are returned as leaves for the application to merge — for the cart, by union, so a deleted item can reappear though nothing is lost. What was given up is not joins or a query language but having one place where the meaning of conflicting truths is decided. That moved into application code, and the merge rule chosen there is the consistency model users actually experience.
